episodes.212837: Slightly higher moisture behind a backdoor front combined with intense daytime heating on June 18th resulting in the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across the higher terrain during the afternoon and early evening hours. One thunderstorm near Abo and Mountainair produced a wet microburst induced severe wind gust at a personal weather station on the Dear Canyon Preserve. Higher moisture remained in place along and east of the central mountain chain on June 19th resulting in another round of scattered thunderstorms across the central mountain chain and adjacent highlands during the afternoon hours. Severe thunderstorms dropped large hail in San Jose, produced a wet microburst induced severe wind gust northeast of Vaughn, and severe wind gusts near Tolar. Thunderstorms tapered off around sunset both days due to the loss of daytime heating.
episodes.213101: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
episodes.213158: Moisture associated with Tropical Storm Arthur approached Central Alabama on June 17 into June 18. On June 17, several showers and low-topped supercells developed over southeastern Central Alabama. One cell produced a well-defined funnel cloud in southeastern Lowndes County that was caught in at least two videos posted to social media. The next day, heavy rainfall near Chalkville led to a portion of Sweeny Hollow Rd being flooded.||In the wake of the remnants of Arthur passing through Central Alabama on June 18, a cold front entered the area and became stalled. On June 19, heavy rainfall became concentrated along a boundary along and south of the U.S. 80 corridor, leading to flooding issues in Pike and Lowndes counties. By June 20, the stalled front over Central Alabama reignited training thunderstorms along the U.S. 280 and I-22 corridors, with heavy rainfall of 2 to 5 inches causing flash flooding in the Birmingham metro area during the afternoon hours.
episodes.213273: Late on the night of June 18, coverage of showers and thunderstorms expanded in association with a cold front and a slow-moving shortwave trough. This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. As the front continued southward and the shortwave propagated eastward, a second round of showers and storms developed across Central Texas on Saturday, June 20. The primary hazard accompanying these storms was flash flooding, though a few instances of damaging winds were also reported.
episodes.213359: A front moving through a very hot airmass brought a line of strong storms to the marine environment off of the coast of the Carolinas.
episodes.213360: The persistence of a heat wave paired with weak upper level disturbances lead to another severe storm-related downing of trees.
episodes.213456: Widespread showers and storms developed across south-central and southeast Kansas during the morning hours of June 18th. These storms continued to fester across southern Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours. While no damaging wind was reported, the strongest of these storms produced quarter to golf ball size hail.
episodes.213457: A line of thunderstorms pushed southeastward across central Kansas and the Flint Hills during the evening hours of June 19. These storms produced up to quarter size hail and 75 mph winds.
episodes.213604: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moves through the area especially across Hennepin and Ramsey Countines. Due to the rate and quantity of hailstones, a few areas had observed hail accumulation on the ground. The largest hailstone diameter was 2.25 inches observed 2 miles NNE of St. Paul.
episodes.213605: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota and then western Wisconsin saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moved through the area, covering the ground completely at times.||The second round of storms followed about 30 to 60 minutes behind and produced scattered wind damage to trees and a few power lines. The very southern portion of Eau Claire County saw a highly visible funnel cloud near Osseo, which briefly touched down on the west side of town near the Merchants Baseball Field off US Highway 10. This tornado falls within NWS La Crosse's forecast jurisdiction, and more detail on the tornado can be found there.
episodes.213813: An incoming front helped generate showers and thunderstorms across (mainly southern) portions of the area. A narrow band of convection developed along I-20, spanning from around the I-10 and I-20 split towards Odessa. Flash flooding was reported in Pecos and in Monahans due to this narrow band of heavy rainfall.
episodes.213848: A trough pattern moved into the area on the 18th. This lead to an increase in thunderstorm activity, with isolated storms mainly near the Sierra and into northeast CA. The strongest storms produced a peak gust around 60 mph near Meyers, along with reports of hail up to 0.75 inches in diameter.
episodes.213851: A trough pattern moved into the area on the 18th and 19th. On the 19th, a cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms produced widespread lightning (over 2500 strikes), heavy rainfall of 1 to over 2 inches and several reports of flash flooding in western NV from Stagecoach to southeast Reno/Hidden Valley, east Sparks to Lockwood and Spanish Springs. Hail up to 1��� diameter and wind gusts of 60-75+ mph also occurred with these storms as they pushed across northwest and west central NV.
episodes.214009: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
episodes.214016: A summer pattern of south to southwestern mean flow, combined with impacts from both the Gulf and Atlantic sea breezes and PWATs near or above 2 inches, resulted in numerous thunderstorms across northeast FL.
episodes.214072: An incoming cold front from the northwest interacted with moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur lifting northeast from the Gulf coast on the 18th of June. This lead to widespread showers across much of the forecast area, but especially so over our Virginia counties, resulting in a few flooding reports. An isolated severe storm embedded in a line led to isolated wind damage.
episodes.214147: An approaching cold front and trough of low pressure combined with a very unstable airmass producing conditions conducive to robust thunderstorm development. Showers and thunderstorms developed across the Coastal Plain and along the immediate coast of South Carolina and quickly pushed northeastwards tracking mainly east of Hwy 17 and along the coastal waters of Eastern North Carolina while strengthening during the late morning to early afternoon hours of June nineteenth. A few of these storms became severe in nature and brought strong winds to the Crystal Coast and Pamlico Sound.
episodes.214350: A strong warm air advection pattern and low-level jet fostered widespread thunderstorm activity across western-north Texas into southwestern Oklahoma on the early morning of the 19th. A few briefly intense thunderstorm cores produced observations of severe winds during this time.
episodes.214351: A strong warm air advection pattern and low-level jet fostered widespread thunderstorm activity across western-north Texas into southwestern Oklahoma on the early morning of the 19th. A few briefly intense thunderstorm cores produced observations of severe winds during this time.
episodes.214467: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.214523: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front across northern Minnesota during the afternoon of the 19th. A few of the storms produced quarter to golf ball-sized hail in the Brainerd Lakes area into the I-35 corridor as they moved through.
episodes.214551: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
episodes.214613: A cold front brought severe weather, heavy rain, and flash flooding to southeast Alabama.
episodes.214656: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 18-22 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported along with flash flooding.
episodes.214660: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
episodes.214757: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley bordering Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Northeast Texas, and into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours of June 19th, with a warm, very moist and unstable air mass present across East Texas along and south of the front. An upper level disturbance traversed atop the front during the morning and early afternoon hours, enhancing large scale forcing for the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along and south of the front. Given the very moist air mass in place, these storms were very efficient rainfall producers, with widespread rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling over Central and Northern Red River and Bowie Counties in Northeast Texas. These excessive rainfall amounts in a short period of time resulted in reports of flash flooding across these areas, particularly in the Detroit and Dekalb areas with multiple roads flooded and water entering homes.
episodes.214856: Thunderstorms developed across parts of eastern ND and one severe thunderstorm produced quarter size hail in Cass County, ND.
episodes.214857: A low top supercell developed in Hubbard county and produced an EF-0 tornado near Laporte, MN during the afternoon.
episodes.214979: A weak surface frontal boundary slowly shifted south across extreme Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas during the morning and afternoon hours on June 19th, separating warm and very moist air near and south of the front from the slightly drier air to the north. A weak upper level disturbance traversed east atop the front throughout the morning into the early afternoon hours, which enhanced large scale forcing for the development of showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall. As this continued through the morning, the periods of heavy rain moved repeatedly over the same areas, which resulted in widespread amounts of 2-4+ inches falling over Northern Miller County Arkansas. These totals fell in a very short period of time, which resulted in high rushing water from Nix Creek flooding the back portion of an apartment complex off of Arkansas Road in Texarkana Arkansas. The high water also stalled at least one vehicle in the parking lot and forced the evacuation of several homes in the area.
episodes.215012: Isolated severe storms over the Black Hills and and portions of northwest SD produced some damaging wind gusts.
episodes.215077: A weak front was stalled across northern Mississippi on June 19, 2026. Moist and unstable air pooled south of the front with SBCAPEs greater than 3000 J/kg. A cluster of thunderstorms developed along the front and produced isolated wind damage.
episodes.215139: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
episodes.215473: Thunderstorms brought isolated flash flooding to the Heartland.
episodes.215696: A thunderstorm produced gusty winds late in the evening in the lower Chesapeake Bay and Lower James River June 18.
episodes.215715: Southeast surface winds pushed moisture all the way through far west Texas with an upper level disturbance moving southeast through the area brought strong to severe thunderstorms to Hudspeth County.
episodes.215725: During the evening hours on June 19th, a couple of severe storms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts and two brief tornadoes. One of these storms trekked through Trempealeau County where it produced golf ball sized hail in Osseo as well as a weak EF-0 tornado which resulted in minor damage. An additional tornado was documented in Jackson County, but no damage was verified which resulted in an EF-U rating.
episodes.215730: Afternoon thunderstorms embedded within weakly sheared and moderately unstable, deep layer south to southwest flow produced wind damage near Lake Placid in Highlands County.
episodes.215864: Additional heavy rainfall along with wet antecedent conditions lead to more flash flooding, some significant, in the Pine Belt region of Mississippi. Several major roads were flooded, as well as homes. Water rescues were conducted in the Seminary area as several cars became stranded.
episodes.215878: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across coastal waters.
episodes.215879: A moist southwest flow between low pressure passing well inland and high pressure offshore led to an environment supportive of strong thunderstorms across warm Atlantic waters.
episodes.215910: Multiple offshore-moving thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the coast.
episodes.215968: A moist southwest flow between low pressure passing well inland and high pressure offshore led to an environment supportive of strong thunderstorms near the Southeast South Carolina coast.

An EF0 tornado with winds of 85 MPH tracked north to south across Arabi, LA in St. Bernard Parish. This was confirmed via eyewitness videos, along with debris thrown to the SE and convergent debris in that direction. Almost all of the damage was shingles off well built homes, fence damage and large branches down. Three houses had a good part of their roof removed. Two were older houses, one built in the 50s. One house had a car port attached to the roof which is where the failure occurred. The third was abandoned and neighbors confirmed it also had extensive termite damage. That and rot was observed on the roof. Given that well built homes had minor damage and the damage on the three houses were from older roofs, the rating is an 85 MPH EF0.
